title: Land Is Not a Commodity: Why a Land Value Tax Can Cure the Housing Crisis
dek: The housing shortage is only a symptom; the real disease is land monopoly. A land value tax shifts the burden off buildings and onto land, forcing hoarders to develop or sell, and returning location value to society instead of fattening landlords.
why: The land value tax is an overlooked lever that economists on both left and right agree on. Lars Doucet turns an abstract tax mechanism into a power struggle, using Houston parking lots, South Korea's appraisal system, and Norway's resource dividend as cases.
who: Economists who care about housing policy, urban planners, real estate developers, and investors and policy researchers who want to know whether the land tax is worth betting on.

points.h: A land tax is not a property tax, it is a location tax
points.body: Lars builds his case on one analogy: the land value tax shares an origin with the ordinary property tax, but it splits ‘building value’ from ‘land value’. A building tax punishes you for constructing, maintaining, and renovating; a land tax only punishes you for holding a good location and letting nothing grow on it. He says land value comes from the labor of the people around you — your ability to earn a living, go to school, and make friends the moment you walk out the door depends entirely on your neighbors and the whole city. The landlord lies there and sucks this collective value into his own pocket, and that is the paradox of Progress and Poverty: the ballpoint pen fell from $270 to 11 cents, but land never does.

points.h: The builders are right, but not right enough
points.body: The host asks: Oakland relaxed density and rents fell, so do we still need a land tax? Lars concedes that the ‘housing shortage’ is the main cause, but points out that the YIMBY camp never explains one counterexample: Houston has no zoning, yet its downtown still holds a giant surface parking lot worth $500 million. Why? Because the property tax bundles land and buildings together, so the more you build the more tax you pay, while sitting on it and waiting for appreciation is actually cheaper. So developers have no incentive to develop, only an incentive to lobby for rezoning and then keep hoarding. He says a reform without a land tax ends in the stalemate of ‘you rezoned it, but I just won't sell’.

points.h: The objections are built on imagination
points.body: Lars sorts the opposition into three categories and takes them apart one by one. How do you appraise land separately from buildings? He says 14,000 assessment jurisdictions worldwide already do something like it: South Korea manually reviews 500,000 sample parcels a year and produces nationwide land values in 5 months; Norway trained a national automated valuation model on the state property data platform Finn.no with a core team of just 3 people. Think there will be too many protests? He says the real source of protest is ‘the land looks the same as next door, why charge me more’ — under a land tax, you and your neighbor are assessed on the same location basis, which actually makes it easier to compute. The excuse for not doing it is that nobody has measured it.

points.h: The little old lady is not an argument against it
points.body: The sharpest criticism is ‘the transition is unfair’ — on the day a land tax is announced, existing landowners instantly bear the capitalized value of all future tax liability, which amounts to expropriation in one stroke. Lars concedes this is a Gordon Tullock-style transition trap, then offers the guardrail: the move is never a one-step nationwide 100% land tax, but a gradual switch by school district or by county; run revenue-neutral simulations and most single-family homes actually see their tax bill fall. As for the elderly afraid of being driven out of their old homes, he says Texas has long had a tax deferral system: you owe it, and after death it is deducted with interest from the estate.

points.h: Britain's failure was a capacity problem
points.body: The most commonly cited counterexample online is Britain's 1910s ‘People's Budget’: the valuation took 6 years and was overturned by shopkeepers' protests and the courts. Lars's response is blunt: that much-shared article is simply ‘deriving a universal law from 1 sample’, and it simultaneously claims that ‘a pure land tax has never succeeded’ and that ‘land cannot be valued’ — yet South Korea has been appraising nationwide land values parcel by parcel for decades. He says this only proves the British state machine was weak, not that a land tax is theoretically unworkable. His tone hardens: if you want to be a serious critic, go find counterexamples, instead of passing off lazy ignorance as a verdict.

points.h: Norway achieved Georgism through a resource dividend
points.body: Lars points to a fact that makes Norway a ‘success story’ today: Norway's entire national resource management regime is Georgist in structure — natural resources such as oil are recognized as the property of all the people, and extractors pay extremely high resource taxes, yet production and investment themselves are not punished, so it encourages entrepreneurship while channeling the natural bounty into the treasury to fund universal welfare. Norway's Georgism is almost perfect, except that it is not on land value. This ‘Norwegian paradox’ leads him to assert: the land tax is not the enemy of the welfare state, it can be its foundation.

points.h: The automobile opened a second frontier
points.body: Lars explains why the land question that filled the air 100 years ago later vanished: the frontier itself is a mechanism of ‘free land’ — as long as you can still expand into the wilderness, the people at the bottom don't have to face the squeeze of ‘high wages plus high rent’. America's first frontier was westward expansion, and when it closed Henry George appeared; in the 20th century the automobile turned the suburbs into a ‘second frontier’ and extended things another 80 years, until it closed again around 2006-2008. He says what people now call a ‘second Gilded Age’ is just a script from over a hundred years ago with a new cast, and post-pandemic remote work, as a ‘third frontier’, held out for roughly 5 minutes before capital digested it.

points.h: Don't win online, do the politicians' homework
points.body: The closing answer to the last question is very concrete: Lars says the most effective way to create change he has learned in the past 5 years is not arguing with keyboard warriors, but taking every objection a state senator or city council member might raise, running the data simulations and preparing the answers in advance, and putting them directly on their desks — he calls ‘doing politicians' homework’ an absurd but extraordinarily effective strategy. Several states have already passed bills allowing land value tax reform. His call to action: go measure, don't guess.

terms.def: An annual tax levied on the value of land rather than the total value of a property, which does not punish building improvements.
The 19th-century school of thought launched by Henry George: land is common wealth, and land rent should be captured by society.
The movement that advocates loosening land-use zoning rules and allowing more housing to be built.
Using a unified model and sample parcels to value properties automatically across a whole jurisdiction, rather than assessing each one on site.
The Georgist ideal: tax only land value and abolish all other taxes on labor and capital.
The high rents extracted from natural resources (such as oil), collected on behalf of all citizens.
